title: MIDI Scale, Arpeggio, and Notation Workflow for Orchestral and Band Instruments
goal: Create and refine a MIDI mapping and scale-generation workflow for instrument patches, including playable range checks, scale logic, timing logic, file organization, and later sheet-music output that could be used in a DAW-based production context.
context: I chose this goal because it reflects a real part of the kind of technical music work I do: defining playable ranges, building scale-based MIDI material, checking naming and organization, and then evaluating whether the output is actually usable in a production context. For a non-expert, the workflow is basically part music theory, part file generation, and part quality control. The task was not just “make MIDI files”; it involved deciding what should be included for each instrument, checking timing math, correcting naming conventions, revising output organization, and later moving into more stylistic and notation-based requests when the first outputs opened up new directions for the work.

session_goal_achievement.Why or why not: Yes, but only partially in a polished sense. Claude did generate the core MIDI and notation outputs I asked for, and it was especially helpful with timing math, batch generation, and handling large structured output sets. At the same time, some of the later musical/stylistic outputs needed revision, the organizational side of the files was not always ideal on the first pass, and the mood-based material did not consistently make sense across the board.

Step 1.step_name: Define the instrument scope, playable ranges, and chromatic plan.
Step 1.step_action: Participant asked for standard-velocity MIDI scales for Piano, Nylon Guitar, Viola, Violin, Cello, and Trumpet Bb, one note per bar, one-second-per-bar timing goal. Claude caught that 80 BPM/4-4 wouldn't give 1s bars, proposed 60 BPM/1-4, laid out assumed practical ranges per instrument, generated chromatic runs.

nodes.label: Request MIDI scales across six instruments with a specific velocity and timing spec
nodes.detail: Asked Claude for separate standard-velocity MIDI scale files for Piano, Nylon Guitar, Viola, Violin, Cello, and Trumpet Bb. Specified one note per bar at 80 BPM, intending each bar to equal one second.

nodes.label: Correct tempo math, define instrument ranges, and generate verified chromatic scale MIDI files
nodes.detail: Pointed out that 80 BPM in 4/4 gives 3-second bars not 1, and proposed 60 BPM in 1/4 time so each bar equals exactly one second. Laid out assumed practical playable ranges for each of the six instruments, flagging them for confirmation. Built chromatic runs across each instrument's assumed range at constant velocity, verified that each file's duration matched its note count in seconds, and delivered all six MIDI files with GM program-change assignments noted.

nodes.detail: Searched the web for common pop key signatures and chord-progression practices from 2020–2026, used the findings to narrow the arpeggio scope to 18 musically meaningful keys rather than all 48 possible, then built 90 arpeggio files (18 keys × 5 moods), verified the note range stayed within a sensible piano register, cleaned up stray leftover files, and explained the rhythmic/velocity design behind each mood.

Packaged and delivered the corrected 60-file block-chord batch, explaining the distinct voicing and rhythmic comping pattern designed for each mood (e.g. power-chord voicing for anger, off-beat hits for tense).

Claude asked clarifying questions, did timing math for a 5-second event length, built sequential scale files and stacked chord files organized into nested folders by instrument and key.

nodes.detail: Specified sequential scale files plus a separate huge-chord version for each, and defined the band lineup as Electric Guitar, Bass, Piano/Keys, and Vocals (skipping drums for lack of fixed pitch).

Confirmed chord files were exactly 5.0 seconds and sequential files scaled correctly with note count, then packaged the material into three section zips (band, strings, brass) and explained the folder structure and range assumptions.

Step 5.step_name: Document the workflow and final output.
Step 5.step_action: Participant asked for clean sheet music with correct clef placement. Claude pushed back on notating huge cluster chords, proposed narrowing to chromatic sweeps, installed LilyPond, generated engraved notation for 12 instruments with instrument-appropriate clefs/transpositions. Participant then said the piano sheet music could be visually clearer — Claude was mid-response when the recording/transcript ends.

nodes.detail: Explained that the giant stacked cluster-chord files would only render as an unreadable wall of ledger lines, and that notating all 1,176 source files wasn't practical. Checked that LilyPond engraving software was installable and asked which files should get sheet music.

nodes.label: Install LilyPond, build a notation generator, verify tricky cases, and deliver 12 engraved PDFs
nodes.detail: Installed the LilyPond engraving software and wrote a generation script assigning instrument-appropriate clefs (including dynamic clef changes) and transpositions for each of the 12 instruments. Test-compiled the guitar file first and visually inspected the rendered ottava clef, then compiled all 12 instruments and spot-checked the trickiest cases: the piano grand staff, cello's bass-tenor-treble clef changes, and trumpet transposition. Packaged all 12 instrument PDFs engraved with LilyPond rather than a raw MIDI-to-notation converter, and explained the clef/transposition convention used for each instrument along with the choice to use plain quarter notes as a reference chart rather than a literal timing transcription.

Step 1.step_name: Define the instrument scope, playable ranges, and chromatic plan.

Step 1.input: Instrument list, timing requirement, playable-range concept
Step 1.output: A defined task scope with selected instruments, assumed practical ranges, and chromatic MIDI outputs built around the corrected one-second-per-bar timing.
rubrics: The selected instruments and their playable ranges are clearly identified.
The tempo and bar-length math are corrected and made internally consistent.
The chromatic outputs reflect a practical range-testing approach.
The outputs are usable as a starting point for later scale-generation work.
The initial organization is clear enough to continue without major confusion.

ratings.output_quality_reason: Claude caught the timing issue right away, explained it clearly, and generated usable chromatic files across the requested instruments. This part of the session was efficient and technically solid, even though some ranges were still assumptions that would need later confirmation if I wanted stricter realism.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: It correctly identified the timing mismatch in my original spec, proposed a usable fix, and generated the first round of playable-range chromatic files, giving me a solid foundation for the rest of the session.

Step 2.step_name: Build the scale and note-mapping logic.
Step 2.step_action: Participant asked for all major scales on piano, then major/natural-minor/diminished/augmented scales across all instruments. Claude made theory/naming choices (natural minor, whole-half diminished, augmented hexatonic), later adjusted enharmonic naming per participant feedback.
Step 2.input: Confirmed piano output, request for all major scales, expansion to other instruments and scale types, feedback on enharmonic naming
Step 2.output: A working scale-generation plan and large batch of MIDI files organized by instrument and scale type, including major, natural minor, diminished, augmented, and earlier chromatic outputs.
rubrics: Notes stay within the stated playable range for each instrument.
Scale content is theoretically consistent with the requested type.
Enharmonic naming and file labeling are musically sensible.
The output set is organized clearly enough to review and use.
The mapping logic is documented clearly enough that I can follow the assumptions being made.

ratings.output_quality_reason: Claude handled the scale generation at a large scale and documented the underlying assumptions, which made the work traceable. The reason this is not a 5 is that some naming and theory choices needed correction or clarification from me, and the organizational side of the output was not as clean as I would have wanted on the first pass.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: It generated the requested scale sets across instruments and was transparent about the theory assumptions it made, which let me redirect it when needed. It did require intervention on naming and later on organization, so the success here was real but not completely frictionless.

rubrics: The MIDI outputs follow the requested harmonic or rhythmic format.
The mood-based variations make musical sense.

ratings.output_quality_reason: This was the most mixed part of the session. Claude was productive and fast, and it did generate a lot of material, but the mood-based outputs did not make sense consistently across the board, and one major revision was needed because the first chord-progression batch was still arpeggiated when I had explicitly asked for stacked chords. The final corrected block-chord batch was more usable than the first pass.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: The first pass missed an important distinction between broken-chord motion and actual chord progressions played as stacked chords. Once corrected, Claude acknowledged the miss, rebuilt the files, and produced a more appropriate output.

Step 4.output: Large, structured playable-range packages across band, string, and brass instruments, with timing standardized to 96 BPM in 4/4 for 2 bars = 5 seconds, including both sequential and stacked-chord versions.

ratings.output_quality_reason: Claude handled the timing math well, asked clarifying questions before generating a huge amount of material, and produced the requested large-scale packages. The reason this is not a 5 is that the sheer amount of output still created organizational friction, and some of the work was only as useful as the review structure around it.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: It clarified scope before generating hundreds of files, did the duration math correctly, and delivered the requested sequential and chord-based versions in a structured way. The main limitation was not failure to generate, but how much review was still needed because of the scale of the output.

ratings.output_quality_reason: The notation output was one of the more thoughtful parts of the session because Claude recognized where literal transcription would fail, narrowed scope appropriately, and used proper engraving software. I did still have clarity concerns about the piano presentation, and the transcript ends before that last refinement is completed, so I would not score it as fully finished.

goal_achievement.Did you achieve your goal after ~1-hour: Yes, with an unfinished final revision
goal_achievement.Why or why not: It handled the notation task intelligently, used the right tool for clean engraving, and responded well to constraints about readability. The only reason this is not a clean “yes” without qualification is that the final piano-specific revision was interrupted before I got the updated result.
